item.title: Performing Globalization — Trade and Industry
item.description:
It’s Not (Just) the Tariffs: Rethinking Non-Tariff Measures in a Fragmented Global Economy
Daria Taglioni & Hiau Looi Kee
World Bank Research Observer, August 2026, Pages 223-241

Abstract:
Tariff protection has declined substantially over recent decades, even though tariffs increased in some countries in 2025. Trade restrictions have not disappeared; they have changed form. Non-tariff measures (NTMs) have become central instruments of trade policy, particularly in high-income countries and in highly regulated sectors. Many NTMs pursue legitimate objectives such as food safety, environmental protection, and consumer protection. Yet they also shape market access in less visible ways. Because compliance costs vary widely, NTMs can act as capability-based filters that sort exporters according to regulatory capacity, technological sophistication, and export structure. Drawing on recent advances in estimating ad valorem equivalents (AVEs), this paper examines how the growing importance of NTMs relative to tariffs alters effective protection. Three patterns emerge. Higher-income countries rely relatively more on NTMs than on tariffs; exporters from low- and middle-income countries face higher effective protection in advanced markets; and NTMs disproportionately burden smaller firms, increasing the likelihood of export exit and potentially contributing to greater market concentration. Together, these mutually reinforcing patterns highlight the importance of transparency, careful policy design, and regulatory cooperation to ensure NTMs achieve legitimate objectives without reinforcing fragmentation or inequality in global trade.

Closing Ranks: Organized Labor and Immigration
Carlo Medici
Journal of Political Economy, forthcoming

Abstract:
This paper shows that immigration fostered the emergence of American organized labor. I digitize archival records to assemble the ﬁrst county-level dataset on historical U.S. unionization and use a shift-share instrument to isolate plausibly exogenous labor supply shocks induced by immigration, between 1900 and 1920. Counties with higher immigration experienced increases in union presence and membership. These effects were more pronounced among skilled workers, particularly in counties more exposed to immigrant labor competition, and in areas with more negative attitudes toward immigrants. The evidence is consistent with existing workers unionizing in response to immigration, driven by economic and social motivations.

Gender-Role Traditionalism and Opposition to Trade in the United States
Andrew Kerner & Jane Sumner
PS: Political Science & Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
A recently popular line in American trade politics is that free trade threatens male blue-collar manufacturing employment, thereby undermining “traditional” family gender roles in which men work outside of the home and women work as caregivers within it. This study asks whether American mass politics mirrors these ideas. Does a preference for “traditional” gender roles lead Americans to protectionism? Our analysis of American National Election Studies data suggests that it does. We find a significant and highly robust empirical relationship between gender conservatism and protectionism. That relationship has been evident since 2008 and it decidedly is not a product of Trump-era politics. That relationship holds among men and women and among Republicans and Democrats, and it is robust to the inclusion of controls meant to isolate gender conservatism from other expressions of conservatism. The recent rise of gender-conservative trade skepticism should be understood as elite politics catching up with the public rather than leading it.

Why is trade not free? A revealed preference approach
Rodrigo Adão et al.
Econometrica, forthcoming

Abstract:
A prominent explanation for why trade is not free is politicians’ desire to protect some of their constituents at the expense of others. In this paper we develop a methodology that can be used to reveal the welfare weights that a nation’s import tariffs implicitly place on different groups of society. Applied in the context of the United States in 2017, this method implies that redistributive trade protection accounts for about a third of US tariff variation and that it causes large monetary transfers between US individuals, mostly driven by differences in welfare weights across sectors of employment. In terms of political economy mechanisms, the welfare weights that we estimate are consistent with lobbying being a significant driver of US trade protection. Perhaps surprisingly, swing states in US presidential elections play a much smaller role.

The Role of Trade in Premature Deindustrialization and Industry Polarization
Michael Sposi, Kei-Mu Yi & Jing Zhang
Econometrica, September 2026, Pages 1779-1815

Abstract:
We document two key patterns of structural change: premature deindustrialization and rising industry polarization. Using a dynamic open-economy model with sector-biased technological change (SBTC), we evaluate the role of trade in these shifts. Trade alone does not cause premature deindustrialization, but its interaction with SBTC -- transmitting global technological change, amplifying the decline in manufacturing's relative price over time, and generating manufacturing trade imbalances across countries -- deepens premature deindustrialization over time. Industry polarization, by contrast, emerges only through trade-driven specialization, as countries diverge along lines of comparative advantage.

Shipping to America
Xiwen Bai et al.
NBER Working Paper, September 2026

Abstract:
We study the macroeconomic and trade-policy implications of disruptions to U.S.-bound shipping routes. Standard models treat them as iceberg-cost shocks, conflating the shock with the response to it. Using satellite vessel-tracking data, we construct route-level measures of potential and effective capacity for all U.S.-bound container ships from 2016 to 2025. Utilization losses in recent disruptions ran 20 to 40 percentage points, and began months before port congestion became visible. We embed these measures in a general equilibrium model in which firms reallocate a common fleet without internalizing the congestion they create and price above marginal cost, while importers' sourcing responds to route profitability. The reallocation triggered by a disruption then has first-order welfare effects, and the route's Domar weight is not a sufficient statistic for its welfare cost. The 2021 West Coast crisis and the 2023-2024 Red Sea attacks cost 0.69% and 0.35% of output. Naval protection of Red Sea shipping generated benefits of 0.04-0.08% of output at a fiscal cost of 0.02%. Tariffs decongest the routes they tax, offsetting or even reversing their conventional welfare cost.

Borrowing in the Shadow of China
Illenin Kondo, César Sosa-Padilla & Zachary Swaziek
NBER Working Paper, September 2026

Abstract:
China's rise as a major lender to emerging economies since the early 2000s has introduced a unique form of lender power: borrowers cannot default on the subsidized loans they receive, but may still face sudden rollover demands outside their control. We argue this distinctive structure -- bilateral rollover risk without default risk -- disciplines recipient countries' borrowing on international markets. In a quantitative long-term sovereign debt model, we show that such rollover-prone nondefaultable Chinese loans expose market debt to dilution risk: governments may need to tap international lenders when repayment to China comes due, and therefore choose to deleverage from private markets when Chinese inflows arrive. Market debt and bond yield dynamics in the data are consistent with this “disciplining effect.” We then use the model to study two geopolitical scenarios: a bloc-formation exercise in which China offers take-it-or-leave-it loans to induce the borrower's exit from international debt markets, and an optimal exposure-to-China problem under the risk of a permanent and sudden retrenchment of Chinese funding. Together, these results show how official finance à la China can simultaneously improve market borrowing conditions and become a new destabilizing force to the global sovereign debt architecture as geopolitical alliances shift.

item.title: How Typical — Stereotypes and Norms
item.description:
Why Most Stereotypes Are Negative
Christian Unkelbach, Anne Irena Weitzel & Hans Alves
Psychological Review, forthcoming

Abstract:
Stereotypes are a foundational construct in psychological science, often defined as beliefs concerning characteristic group attributes. We present a cognitive-ecological theory of social perception that predicts and explains why such characteristic attributes are likely negative, that is, why most stereotypes are negative. The theory assumes that, cognitively, people characterize groups by attributes that distinguish them from other groups. Ecologically, positive social information is more frequent (i.e., positivity prevalence), and negative social information is more diverse (i.e., negativity diversity). If negative attributes are less frequent and more diverse relative to positive attributes, then they must be more likely to distinguish one group from another. Consequently, the attributes people see as characteristic of a group are likely to be negative. We illustrate the predicted stereotype negativity across two studies and two existing data sets. We then formalize the theory and illustrate it with simulations showing that rare attributes can be highly diagnostic of group membership while applying to only a minority of group members. Thus, the theory explains why most stereotype content is likely negative, despite the well-documented positivity prevalence, and why stereotypes may be diagnostic and comparatively accurate, despite being descriptively inaccurate. The theory explains stereotype negativity without requiring motivational derogation, essentialist group differences, or a general negativity bias, and it clarifies when positive stereotypes should occur. We also discuss the theory’s relation to dimensional models of stereotype content and consequences for interventions aimed at reducing stereotype negativity.

“A girl is the champion!”: Well-intentioned gendered messages can backfire
April Bailey, Maya Kreitman & Andrei Cimpian
Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, October 2026, Pages 2581-2600

Abstract:
Initiatives aimed at promoting gender equity in majority-male domains often emphasize gender to highlight women’s achievements (e.g., “Space4Women,” “all-women spacewalk”). Does such gendered messaging help achieve equity goals? Two theoretical accounts offer competing predictions. An informational account suggests that referencing a gender alongside a domain should strengthen beliefs that the referenced gender participates and succeeds. A pragmatic account, however, predicts that explicitly marking gender may backfire by signaling that the referenced gender is atypical in the domain -- otherwise, why mention it? We tested these two possibilities with U.S. children (ages 4–10; N = 326) and adults (N = 788). Participants learned about fictional activities described with either gendered messaging (e.g., “A girl/boy is the Gazzer champion”) or control messaging (e.g., “Joan/Rob is the Gazzer champion”). Gendered messaging backfired compared to control messaging on average, causing participants to infer lower participation by the referenced gender and, among adults, lower ability. Gendered messaging also undermined participants’ interest in the activities. A meta-analysis across experiments revealed small-to-moderate effects that were larger for adults than children, consistent with developmental changes in pragmatic reasoning. Finally, backfire effects disappeared for messaging about fictional groups, suggesting that background knowledge about the referenced group may be needed to trigger pragmatic inferences. Together, these findings advance theoretical accounts of pragmatic reasoning while indicating that well-intentioned gendered messaging may paradoxically undermine equity goals. A more effective alternative may be to clearly feature women in a domain without explicitly framing it as being “for them.”

On Confederate Monuments, Their Removal and Racial Bias
Maximilian Primbs et al.
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, forthcoming

Abstract:
The presence of Confederate monuments and their removal has been a frequent topic of societal discussion in the United States. Taking a situational perspective (i.e. the Bias of Crowds model), the present paper investigated whether the presence of Confederate monuments and their removal from an area causally affect the racial biases of people in that area. Across multiple large-scale data analyses (N1 = 1,753,557), online experiments (N2a = 1,164, N2b = 416, N3 = 537), and a field study (N4 = 176), we found no evidence that the presence or removal of Confederate monuments reliably affects the implicit (or explicit) racial biases of people. We discuss implications for situational models of bias and best research practices for conducting geographical difference studies.

Wrestling with perceptions: How WWE live events in Saudi Arabia shaped views of Muslims in the United States
Rudy Alamillo
Politics, Groups, and Identities, forthcoming

Abstract:
In 2018, the Saudi Ministry of Sport and WWE announced a 10-year agreement to host multiple WWE events in Saudi Arabia to be broadcast around the world. Although these events were intended to drive tourism to Saudi Arabia, they may also have improved attitudes toward Muslims among WWE fans in line with the parasocial contact hypothesis, which argues that positive exposure to members of a minority group through the media can improve feelings toward that group. I test this proposition using two studies. First, an analysis of tweets from professional wrestling fans suggests that relative to fans of another professional wrestling company, WWE fans saw a substantial increase in positive posts about Muslims following WWE's events in Saudi Arabia. Second, using an online survey experiment, I find that exposure to WWE events in Saudi Arabia increased feelings of commonality toward Muslims among WWE fans, which is a key mechanism through which attitude change occurs. Taken together, these results improve our understanding of the parasocial contact hypothesis and provide evidence that under certain conditions, attitude change can occur not just via exposure to positive depictions of well-known members of outgroups, but incidental exposure to outgroups members as well.

The Politics of Black Classification: Sociopolitical Cues and Racial Perception
Lauren Davenport, Hakeem Jefferson & Hunter Rendleman
Perspectives on Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
What makes someone Black in American society today? From Donald Trump questioning Kamala Harris’s racial identity to Joe Biden’s claim that hesitant Black voters “ain’t Black,” American politics frequently brings questions of racial authenticity and belonging to the surface. Yet political science often approaches race as a fixed attribute, rather than a social construction. Here, we seek to understand how Americans define blackness in social and political life. Using a conjoint experiment with a racially diverse sample that includes Black, White, and mixed-race Black-White respondents, we evaluate how ascribed and acquired traits influence perceptions of blackness. The results show that inherited characteristics -- particularly parentage and skin tone, which are the strongest determinants of racial classification -- play a central role, yet sociopolitical cues such as partisanship, neighborhood context, and spousal race also influence racial classification. Using a continuous measure, we also show that respondents make graded assessments of blackness rather than purely binary classifications, with some individuals perceived as more Black than others. Black respondents are more likely than White respondents to classify a broader set of profiles as Black, consistent with a more inclusive understanding of racial membership; however, they also place greater emphasis on shared political identity. These findings clarify how racial categories are socially constructed and why that construction carries real political and social consequences.

Perceived Pandemic Deficits: How COVID-19 Stereotypes Influence Interview Judgments
Cody Cox et al.
Journal of Applied Social Psychology, forthcoming

Abstract:
Following the COVID-19 pandemic, the perception that high school and college students' social skills had been negatively affected by the social-distancing lockdown proliferated. These perceptions may impact the ability of these individuals to succeed in interview settings. In the current study, participants with hiring experience (N = 322) rated a recorded interview and were told the applicant's social skills either had been impacted by the COVID-19 lockdown or that the lockdown had not impacted social skills (in reality, the interview was recorded before the pandemic). Results indicated that participants rated the applicant's interview performance (i.e., eye contact), personality, and potential hireability more poorly when told that COVID-19 impacted social skills as compared to the stereotype mitigation condition. These results were even stronger for extraverted participants, consistent with research indicating that extraverts draw stronger inferences from applicants' eye contact. Our study demonstrates that stereotypes about lockdown during the COVID-19 pandemic harming social development impacted perceived interview performance and that these stereotypes can be mitigated with additional information.

Credible Prejudice? When and Why Mainstream Party Adoption of Far-Right Rhetoric Weakens Anti-Prejudice Norms
Ali Karčić
Political Behavior, forthcoming

Abstract:
This article examines whether mainstream political parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right and how such shifts shape anti-prejudice norms. Building on existing work, I argue that mainstream parties are particularly influential in weakening anti-prejudice norms because they possess greater normative credibility and legitimacy than far-right parties. Empirically, the article combines cross-national observational evidence with two preregistered survey experiments in Germany and Denmark. Using parliamentary speeches from six European countries between 1994 and 2022, I document rising mainstream party anti-Muslim rhetoric and its association with weaker norms against holding far-right views. The experiments provide causal evidence for the argument. In Germany, exposure to prejudiced rhetoric weakens anti-prejudice norms, but only when voiced by mainstream parties, rather than far right parties, likely due to their normative credibility and legitimacy. In Denmark, comparable effects are absent, consistent with decades of mainstream accommodation having already normalized such rhetoric. The experimental results also show that rhetoric targeting Muslims weakens anti-prejudice norms toward out-groups more broadly, suggesting spillover effects. These findings have important implications for future scholarship: when mainstream parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right, they affect not only electoral politics, but also the broader social norm environment.

item.title: Luxuries — Wealth and Inequality
item.description:
How Long Do Wealth Shocks Persist? Less Than Three Generations in England, 1700–2026
Gregory Clark & Neil Cummins
Review of Income and Wealth, November 2026

Abstract:
What happens across generations to wealth shocks? Do they endure and even magnify, or do they dissipate? By implication, how much modern wealth is attributable to events before 1900? This paper uses random shocks to family size in England before 1880 that created wealth shocks for the children to measure the persistence of wealth shocks. Fertility in England before 1880 was a biological lottery. For richer families, family size strongly influenced child wealth. This paper finds that such biology-induced wealth shocks had no impact on descendant wealth by three generations later. Since wealth itself persisted across more than five generations this implies that, in the long run, wealth mainly derives from sources other than inherited wealth. The observed link between nineteenth century and modern wealth does not lie in wealth transfers alone. Wealth persisted because of the familial inheritance of behaviors associated with wealth accumulation and retention.

Structural Injustice as Emergent Disorder
Hochan Kim
American Political Science Review, forthcoming

Abstract:

AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
Nicolò Pagan et al.
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 20 October 2026

Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

Extra-Familial Intergenerational Contact in the Contemporary United States: Exploring Its Frequency, Nature, and Correlates
Craig Fowler & Jessica Gasiorek
Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, forthcoming

Abstract:
Some major studies conducted over the last forty years suggest that intergenerational contact between younger and older adults (i.e., those aged 70+) in Western contexts is scarce. However, the phrasing of questions asked in these studies leaves open the possibility that intergenerational contact might not be so rare. In Study 1 (n = 399), we surveyed young Americans about the frequency and characteristics of their intergenerational interactions. In Study 2 (n = 278), we surveyed a separate sample of young Americans to assess the quantity and communicative quality of their contact with older people, gather information about their intergenerational relationships, and gauge their attitudes towards aging. In Study 1, 42% of respondents had at least one friend aged 70 or older and over 60% had had contact (typically face-to-face) with an older adult during the previous week. In Study 2, the quality and quantity of contact were associated with the endorsement of prescriptive age-based stereotypes, both directly and indirectly via perceptions of common ingroup identity. Moreover, quantity and quality of contact predicted the affective responses younger adults had at the thought of growing old, and their sense of efficacy about doing so. Our results suggest that the state of intergenerational relations in the United States is less dire than some might believe, and that high-quality contact with older adults is associated not only with less negative stereotypes but also younger people feeling both less troubled by and better able to cope with their own aging.

Gender and Interracial Relationship Dissolution: Evidence from a Decade of Roommate Outcomes
Catherine Shea et al.
Social Psychology Quarterly, forthcoming

Abstract:
Using a natural experiment at an elite college (1982–1991), we analyze roommate choices following random first-year assignments, during a period when the Asian-student population doubled. This design allows us to test how shifting demographics affect interracial tie dissolution. Focusing on white-Asian dyads, we find a significant gender divide: Women exhibit consistently high rates of interracial relationship dissolution regardless of population composition, whereas men's interracial ties are affected by population shifts, with tie dissolution increasing as minorities have more same-race outside options. These findings shift the study of intergroup contact from relationship formation to durability, demonstrating that opportunity structures shape interracial relationship dissolution in a setting largely free from self-selection processes that characterize most naturally occurring ties.

The Pain of Ghosting? People Underestimate How Bad Their Conversation Partners Feel About Not Responding
Sophia Li, Coral Zheng & Juliana Schroeder
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, forthcoming

Abstract:
Although online communication platforms provide convenience, they also bring a risk of ghosting, when one person unexpectedly stops responding to another without explanation. Extending prior research that examines the pain of being ghosted, we instead examine whether the act of ghosting itself is emotionally painful -- and whether people recognize the extent of ghosters’ bad feelings. Across three studies -- recalled real ghosting experiences (N = 195), imagined ghosting scenarios (N = 601), and induced ghosting in a live interaction (N = 350) -- we find that people who are ghosted underestimate how bad their conversation partners feel about ghosting them. This underestimation is larger when the ghosting is unintentional and mitigated when communicators do not perceive their actions as ghosting or send a short response (e.g., “sorry, can’t talk”) instead of ghosting. Overall, this research provides a window into the overlooked pain of ghosting others.

More Than a Song: Collective Singing Increases Well-being and Self-Expansion Via Collective Effervescence
Shira Gabriel et al.
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, forthcoming

Abstract:
Humans have been singing with other humans across time and culture. Although past research found positive effects of singing with others, it has not disentangled those effects from being in an established collective. In the current research, we examined the hypothesis that singing in groups leads to increased feelings of well-being and self-expansion even without an established collective. Furthermore, we hypothesized that the main mechanism for these effects is a feeling of collective effervescence -- an intertwining sense that one is connected to others and that something special is happening. Finally, we hypothesized that the positive effects of collective effervescence felt during a singing event can last weeks, even months, after the event. Across two experiments and a longitudinal study, we found support for our hypotheses. Singing in groups predicts positive outcomes (e.g., positive mood, satisfaction with life, self-concept change, donation intentions), primarily via the collective effervescence experienced at these events.

item.title: What a Deal — Products and Consumers
item.description:
The Humanizing Power of Accents in Voicebots: When Accent-Based Humanization Increases User Engagement
Hesam Ghasemi, Amir Sepehri & Cait Lamberton
Journal of Marketing Research, forthcoming

Abstract:
Given that consumers often exhibit resistance toward algorithmic systems, firms face challenges in encouraging engagement with voicebots. In this paper, we find that users’ engagement with voicebots may be enhanced by endowing these tools with non-standard accents that deviate from “standard” pronunciation. Across a range of accents, languages, genders, and contexts, our data suggest that voicebots communicating with non-standard accents make the concept of human diversity salient in the users’ minds. As a result, voicebots communicating with non-standard accents are more readily anthropomorphized. This effect translates into greater preference for the non-standard accented voicebot in customer service settings, stronger support for startups leveraging accented vs. unaccented voicebots, higher willingness to pay for monthly subscriptions, and a greater likelihood of opting in to receive future updates and communications. Consistent with our theory, however, these effects do not hold when the anthropomorphism effect is either overridden by other cues or is undesirable for the consumer. Together, this work highlights the benefits of accented speech in improving human-AI interactions. We also hope that it sparks further investigation into factors that make technology more readily accepted by consumers.

Rong Zhang & Yu Yvette Zhang
Southern Economic Journal, forthcoming

Abstract:

item.title: Teach Me — Schools and Learning
item.description:
Early Grade Retention Harms Adult Earnings
Jiee Zhong
American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, October 2026, Pages 276-308

Abstract:
This paper provides new causal evidence on the effects of grade retention on educational attainment, behavioral outcomes, and labor market performance by analyzing Texas's reading test–based retention policy. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, I find that third-grade retention significantly reduces annual earnings at age 26 by $3,477 (19 percent). While temporarily improving test scores, retention increases absenteeism, violent behavior, and juvenile crime, and reduces the likelihood of high school graduation. Moreover, retained students exhibit higher community college enrollment but lower public university attendance, though neither estimate is statistically significant.

Microdelays disrupt online learning
Asaf Mazar et al.
Nature Human Behaviour, forthcoming

Abstract:
An ever-growing share of education happens on screens. We examine an overlooked feature of modern education: ‘microdelays’ -- brief loading lags that could hinder learners with slower internet connections. In two longitudinal quasi-experimental field studies, microdelays as short as 1–2 s predicted impaired learner engagement and achievement. When faced with microdelays, US primary and secondary school students (N = 26,707) completed fewer online math assignments, took longer to complete assignments, were more likely to get distracted mid-task and earned lower scores. Likewise, when aspiring coders, primarily in Latin America (N = 55,184), experienced microdelays, they spent less time actively engaged, multitasked more often, completed fewer lessons and were less likely to attain a key course milestone. Our results held across a range of model specifications, and leverage within-person variation in load times to support a causal interpretation. These findings identify microdelays as a hitherto-overlooked barrier in online learning.

The Effect of Teacher Experience on Student Test and Non-Test Outcomes: Implications for Educational Policy
Jeongim Jin, Stephen West & Geoffrey Borman
Educational Policy, forthcoming

Abstract:
This study examined the relationship between teacher experience and multiple student outcomes in grades 4 to 6 elementary schools in a large mid-high poverty district. Outcomes considered included standardized state assessments of English language arts and mathematics, social-emotional learning, disciplinary incident count, and disciplinary incident severity. Using multilevel modeling, which adjusted for an extensive set of student and classroom composition covariates, no significant relationship was found between years of teaching and any of the student outcomes. At the student level, state test scores were associated with the student’s prior year test score, giftedness, home language, and English learner status; social-emotional and disciplinary outcomes were associated with race/ethnicity, gender, and special education status. At the classroom composition level, the mean level of the students in the classroom prior year score on the outcome variable was the key predictor of student outcomes. These findings highlight that student factors and classroom composition factors are more predictive of both academic and non-academic student outcomes than teacher experience.

Null Effects of an Intensive Teacher Leadership and Coaching Program at Scale
Michelle Doughty, Mimi Engel & Allison Atteberry
Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, forthcoming

Abstract:
Teacher coaching programs have shown promising effects on student achievement, but these effects vary substantially across programs and seem susceptible to scaling problems. Additionally, the effect of coaching on teacher retention is not known. In this paper, we evaluate a program in which current teachers are released from the classroom part-time to coach and evaluate other teachers. This program was rolled out in five cohorts of schools and eventually reached over 6,000 mentee teachers, presenting a unique opportunity to study the effect of large-scale coaching on teachers and students. We use a difference-in-differences approach with modified estimators to account for the staggered roll-out and find no effects on teacher retention or student test scores.

Disability as Discipline? Effects of the New York City Suspension Ban on Students With Disabilities
Jo King
Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, forthcoming

Abstract:
Suspension bans have become a popular policy response to address excessive and inequitable use of suspension in schools. However, there is little research that examines what strategies school staff employ when suspension is no longer permitted. I examine the effect of New York City’s suspension ban on the use of a potential unintended substitute for suspension: special education classification. I find that the ban induced an increase in disability classifications, especially those with higher social stigma. I show that, on average, students with these classifications experienced large declines in test scores.

Classroom Composition Affects Teacher Performance Ratings
William Delgado & Lauren Sartain
Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, forthcoming

Abstract:
Teacher evaluations should reflect teaching performance rather than the characteristics of the students assigned to a teacher. Exploiting naturally occurring year-to-year variation in classroom composition within teachers, this article examines whether teacher performance ratings assigned by evaluators and students are influenced by classroom context. We find that teachers with higher-achieving and less disruptive students, holding constant the teacher and school, receive systematically higher performance ratings. These effects are robust across model specifications, placebo tests, and multiple dimensions of teaching practice. By contrast, classroom demographics show no consistent association with performance ratings. A policy that adjusts evaluator scores for classroom characteristics, analogous to value-added models, increases the relative ranking of Black teachers by 8 percentage points, highlighting equity impacts of considering classroom context.

Sidewalks for Students: Google Street View Measures of Walkability Around Schools and Chronic Absenteeism Rates
Julia Burdick-Will, Michael Bader & Quynh Nguyen
Educational Researcher, forthcoming

Abstract:
This study brings together ideas from education, public health, and urban planning to assess whether the walkability of the built environment around schools is related to their chronic absenteeism rates. We use national data from the 2018–2019 NCES Common Core of Data and the Office of Civil Rights and computer vision-derived estimates of the physical environment captured in Google Street View Images. We compare schools in the same district to one another and find that schools with a higher proportion of images with sidewalks and streetlights within 1 mile of their location tend to have lower chronic absenteeism rates. These findings support the idea that physical infrastructure can be an important structural barrier to attendance.

Targeted Acceleration in Middle School Math: Impacts on College Entry, Degree Completion, and STEM
David Card & Laura Giuliano
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
We study an accelerated 3-year math curriculum offered in the middle schools of a large urban district that enables students to finish Algebra I and Geometry before high school. Entry to the program is based on 5th-grade math test scores, with a cutoff at the 80th percentile. Continuing eligibility requires at least a B grade in the previous year; successful completion of all three years is highly correlated with an index of non-cognitive skills. Following students for 6 years after high school graduation, we find that the impacts of admission vary widely by non-cognitive skill and gender. Marginally eligible boys with high non-cognitive skills have a 33 percentage point (ppt.) increase in the probability of completing calculus by 11th grade and a 12 ppt. increase in the probability of completing a major in STEM or business within 6 years; boys with lower noncognitive skills take more advanced math classes in high school but have no significant effects on their college outcomes. Like their male peers, marginally eligible girls with high non-cognitive skills are more likely to complete calculus by 11th grade (+17 ppt.). Their rate of graduating with a STEM or business major is unaffected, but they switch from social sciences to the core STEM majors (science, engineering and math). Girls in the two lower terciles of non-cognitive skill are also strongly affected by entry to the program, with higher participation in advanced math classes in high school, higher rates of entry to selective 4-year colleges, and higher rates of completing a STEM or business major (+12 ppt).

Budding enrollment: The impact of cannabis policy on US colleges and universities
Joshua Hess & Danna Thomas
Contemporary Economic Policy, October 2026, Pages 740-766

Abstract:
We examine how liberalized recreational marijuana laws have affected freshmen enrollment and science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) major choice using difference-in-differences and event study models. Estimates indicate near-zero initial enrollment growth as schools substituted between in-state and out-of-state students. However, total enrollment increased in later periods as out-of-state gains persisted and in-state enrollment returned to its baseline. We find little evidence of an adverse effect on total freshmen STEM major enrollment.

NCAA March Madness and Academic Peer Rankings
Sean Mulholland, Kurt Rotthoff & Aleksandar Tomic (Sasha)
Southern Economic Journal, October 2026, Pages 578-595

Abstract:
Building on previous investigations of the relationship between athletic success and school quality, we analyze the effect of appearances, wins, and surprise “Cinderella” runs in the NCAA men's basketball tournament on the peer assessment score of the U.S. News and World Report's annual rankings. We find that reaching the Sweet Sixteen is associated with a peer score increase of 0.3% for National Universities, which is almost equal to the average decline witnessed by National Universities. Peer scores increase by 2.2% for National Liberal Arts Colleges earning a Sweet Sixteen birth, which is 6.1 times the average decline in our National Liberal Arts Colleges sample. Schools making a Cinderella run see a positive boost relative to non-Cinderella teams.

item.title: Higher Power — Religion and Society
item.description:
Residual authoritarianism: Religious dones report the highest levels of left-wing authoritarianism
Daryl Van Tongeren & Shauna Bowes
Psychology of Religion and Spirituality, forthcoming

Abstract:

Religion has been linked with authoritarianism. Although most work has examined religion and right-wing authoritarianism, less work has explored the role of religion in left-wing authoritarianism (LWA). Following the religious residue hypothesis, this preregistered study examined whether residual authoritarianism may be expressed in LWA among those who left religion (i.e., religious dones). Participants (N = 804) completed measures of right-wing authoritarianism and LWA. Currently religious individuals reported the highest levels of right-wing authoritarianism, whereas formerly religious individuals (i.e., religious dones) reported the highest levels of LWA. These results suggest that after leaving religion, authoritarianism remains strong, but its orientation shifts from a right-wing to left-wing expression. Implications for the nuances of religious residue are discussed.

Parental Response to Fetal Shocks and Macroeconomic Volatility
Rakesh Banerjee & Farhan Majid
Review of Economics and Statistics, forthcoming

Abstract:

We examine parental response to a fetal shock using data from 150 Demographic and Health Surveys in 50 developing countries. Focusing on the impact of Ramadan fasting, a common shock experienced by more than a billion Muslims worldwide, we find that children exposed to Ramadan fasting during pregnancy have lower rates of full vaccination for DPT and polio compared to their non-exposed siblings. Further, parents tend to compensate for the fetal shock during booms and reinforce during economic downturns. Our estimations suggest that this has resulted in approximately half a million excess infant deaths over the past three decades.

Belief in the Real Presence Among American Catholics: Prevalence and Patterns
Brad Vermurlen, Mark Regnerus & Anne Morse
Sociological Inquiry, September 2026 

Abstract:

Pew's 2019 poll finding that only three-in-ten American Catholics affirm the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist sparked discussion and concern and was a key motivation for the 3-year National Eucharistic Revival. Using data from a nationally representative 2025 sample of Catholic adults in the United States (N = 1032) and a revised survey item measuring Eucharistic belief, this study provides an updated national estimate of belief in the Real Presence among Catholics. Our estimate is statistically indistinguishable from Pew's 2019 estimate. Moreover, we used logistic regression to identify which demographic, socioeconomic, political, and religious characteristics were most strongly associated with affirming the Real Presence. Frequency of religious service attendance and subjective importance of religious faith were the strongest predictors, whereas most demographic, socioeconomic, regional, and political characteristics mattered little. These findings reveal that belief in the Real Presence among Catholics remains at approximately three-in-ten despite significant catechetical efforts by the Church, and that variation in Eucharistic belief is associated primarily with differences in religious commitment rather than demographics or social location.

Easing the Burden? Religiosity and Educational Inequality in Pain Interference
Laura Upenieks & Markus Schafer
Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion, forthcoming 

Abstract:

A consistent inverse gradient in pain prevalence is typically observed across educational strata. Religion stands out as a source of social and personal support that may moderate the amount of chronic pain interference but may do so differently across the educational spectrum. We test competing hypotheses: The deprivation compensation hypothesis suggests that those suffering from chronic pain with lower education will benefit more from religion, whereas the enhanced resources hypothesis posits that college-educated will receive more benefit. Drawing on Wave 3 of the MIDUS study, we find that among those with chronic pain (N = 1009), respondents with less than a high school degree had the highest chronic pain interference, followed by the high school/General Education Development (GED), some college, or vocational group. Our findings suggest support for the deprivation compensation hypothesis, with religious support and coping displaying a stronger buffering association on pain interference for less educated Americans.

Roberto Fumagalli
Journal for General Philosophy of Science, September 2026, Pages 417-437

Abstract:

In recent years, several prominent authors have criticized fine-tuning arguments for failing to show that the universe’s purported fine-tuning for intelligent life calls for explanation. American Democracy Promotion and the Missionaries of Empire
Jeremy Menchik
Security Studies, forthcoming

Abstract:
While the field of religion and international relations has grown and deepened over the past forty years, this article suggests that scholars have neglected the ways in which religious practices and structural relations shape seemingly secular policies such as democracy promotion. Security scholars have long lamented the adverse effects of democracy promotion, while comprehensive empirical reviews of democracy promotion affirm that it did not increase the likelihood of democratization. If democracy promotion did not spread democracy, what did it do? What was democracy promotion? Drawing on original interviews, research in multiple archives, and a new dataset of grants by the National Endowment for Democracy, the article demonstrates that American democracy promoters were to contemporary American liberal imperialism as Christian missionaries were to European imperialism. Democracy promotion was the ideological component of American liberal imperialism, with democracy promoters playing an analogous role to missionaries seeking to structure the social order. Key practices include universalizing a particular tradition, being sustained by mission rather than outcome, and evangelizing to sustain belief in the home church. In its claims of universality, its use of ideology as a double mask for hegemony, and its deployment of secularized theology, democracy promotion provided the motivation and legitimation for American liberal imperialism. Understanding democracy promotion as the missionary component of American liberal imperialism helps to explain aspects of the policy that were otherwise inexplicable. More theoretically, understanding democracy promotion as the missionary component of American liberal imperialism opens new avenues for scholarship on religion, empire, and international affairs.

The Victory Trap: Endogenous Opposition Coalition Weaknesses in Reversing Autocracy
Elvin Ong & Frances Cayton
Perspectives on Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
After opposition parties and alliances defeat dominant autocratic incumbents, what challenges do they encounter in reversing autocracy and what are the consequences? We argue that long-neglected endogenous weaknesses in opposition coalitions undermine re-democratization efforts, easily opening the door to autocratic comebacks. First, coalition intra-elite conflicts post-victory result in fractured and ineffective governance, generating mass disappointment with the new political elites. Second, coalition intra-supporter divergence pressures the new coalition government into implementing pro-democratic reforms at haphazard speeds and fluctuating scopes. Swift actions in reversing autocracy alienate supporters of the ex-autocrat, elicit accusations of partisan revenge, and fuel counter-mobilization against the new government. A most-different case comparison between the recent autocratic reversal experiences of Poland and Malaysia demonstrates our argument. We show in both cases that ideological and distributional conflicts among diverse coalition elites undermined governance after victory, and different supporter bases prioritized different policy agendas. Counter-mobilization by the autocratic ex-incumbents was highly successful in undermining public support for the new government. These findings suggest that profound challenges in reversing autocracy and rebuilding democracy lie within opposition coalitions themselves, in addition to authoritarian legacies.

One Message, Multiple Functions: Local Propaganda as Bureaucratic Trace Management
Jianjun Yu
Perspectives on Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
This article explores how local government propaganda in China can function as a tool for bureaucratic management. I argue that certain propaganda primarily serves as public documentation of government activities and officials’ performance, enhancing bureaucratic transparency and credibility. This documentation is particularly important when leaders lack personal ties with subordinates and thus require independent verification of their work. However, prioritizing record keeping over public persuasion often produces rigid, unengaging media content, which I term “trace-management propaganda.” Analyzing 1.4 million WeChat posts from Chinese local governments, I demonstrate that trace-management propaganda significantly increases during official evaluation periods and is especially prevalent where personal connections between leaders and subordinates are weak. A difference-in-differences analysis further confirms that a lack of personal ties increases reliance on trace-management propaganda. These findings reveal that local government propaganda in China frequently fulfills both administrative and expressive purposes, providing new insights into state media dynamics and bureaucratic oversight.

Kyklos, forthcoming

Abstract:
Using data from the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) project and the NAVCO catalog (1950–2019), we estimate the developmental effects of successful revolutions through difference-in-differences models and event studies. Our findings differ from common expectations: neither violent nor nonviolent revolutions consistently deliver expected development benefits. Educational indicators remain largely unchanged across both types of revolutions, and both violent and nonviolent movements are associated with lower GDP per capita. Baseline effects on life expectancy are not distinguishable from zero, though some dynamic specifications suggest positive effects for nonviolent revolutions. Our results show that while revolutions may secure political and social gains, the economic costs are large, which raises questions about whether the benefits of revolution justify these development costs.

João Pedro Bastos, Nicolas Cachanosky & Tomás Faintich
Constitutional Political Economy, December 2026, Pages 588-619

Abstract:
Left-leaning populist regimes in 21st-century Latin America have become notoriously long, including some that maintained their power by repealing term limits. Along with changes in external factors, we argue that repealing term limits allowed populist leaders to develop longer time horizons and behave more like stationary than roving bandits. We show that, relative to those constrained by time limits, unconstrained populist leaders mitigate the economic effects of the populist cycle of boom, stagnation, and bust. Populists constrained by term limits act like roving bandits, engaging in more extractive rent-seeking that leads to more significant economic fluctuations.

Roya Izadi
Journal of Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
As international conflicts escalate, states are increasingly turning to conscription and broader public participation in national defense. This article leverages original survey data from Iran, collected before and after the unprecedented April 13, 2024 missile exchange with Israel, to show that the external threat significantly shifted public attitudes toward military service. Using matching techniques to compare responses across the two periods, I find that individuals who were surveyed after the attack were significantly more likely to support mandatory male conscription and women’s military service. Importantly, support rose despite the widespread unpopularity of conscription and Iran’s gender hierarchies. These findings demonstrate that external threats can legitimize coercion in contexts of regime distrust and reconfigure gender boundaries around military participation. The study contributes to research on public perceptions of war, coercion, authoritarian legitimacy and durability, and militarization by highlighting how external threats recalibrate the boundaries of both state authority and gendered citizenship.

Shenghua Lu & Hui Wang
Political Behavior, forthcoming

Abstract:
In the face of property rights violation, why are some groups of people more likely to take collective actions than others? In this paper, we propose that culture is an important but not fully investigated factor accounting for this question. We examine the effect of Confucian clan culture, one of the most far-reaching traditional cultures inherited from ancient China, on collective struggle against land expropriation. We build a unique dataset combining the prefecture-level clan culture intensity and nationwide administrative litigations related to land expropriation between 2014 and 2019. Using the large cross-regional variation in the patterns of administrative litigation and a novel instrumental variable approach, this paper finds that prefectures with stronger clan culture have a significantly larger number of plaintiffs appearing in administrative lawsuit cases, implying that clan culture promotes more pervasive collective actions in confronting state power. Analysis based on individual-level survey data shows that the higher levels of trust between relatives and neighbors and stronger willingness for self-interest-related participation accompanied by stronger Confucian clan culture are the main mechanisms. Our findings underscore the pivotal role of cultural factors in shaping social stability and influencing local governance.

Institutional change and persistence: What does the long-run evidence tell us?
Antonio Savoia, Kunal Sen & Abrams Mbu Tagem
Journal of Institutional Economics, October 2026

Abstract:

This paper provides a systematic econometric investigation of long-run patterns of institutional change, using panel time series methods allowing for different forms of country-specific heterogeneity and cross-section dependence. We focus on variables capturing the quality of four key political and economic institutions over 200 years and 161 countries from the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) database: electoral democracy and executive constraints, for political institutions; and the rule of law and property rights, for economic institutions. We find that political and economic institutions are non-stationary, suggesting that institutional change is more the norm than the exception. We also find that they tend to co-evolve, although this is less evident for property rights, and that long-run causality runs mainly from political to economic institutions. We illustrate the cross-country evidence with discussions on Indonesia and Chile.

Do Judges Move Markets? Ideological Shifts in the Supreme Court and Macroeconomic Expectations
Thomas Drechsel & Naixin Zhang
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
This paper studies how judicial ideology shapes financial markets' expectations about the macroeconomy. We use unexpected deaths of U.S. Supreme Court Justices as quasi-experimental shifts in the Court's ideological balance. High-frequency asset price responses reveal how markets perceive the macroeconomic consequences of these ideological shifts. We find that a more conservative Court is associated with lower inflation expectations, lower real activity expectations, and lower bond yields. A shift towards a more liberal Court induces the opposite responses. The finding that inflation and activity expectations respond with the same sign suggests that markets revise their expectations about aggregate demand, rather than aggregate supply. Moreover, contrasting the yield responses with estimates from studies of fiscal policy news indicates that a more conservative (liberal) Court leads markets to expect tighter (looser) future fiscal policy. We validate our quasi-experimental setup with sectoral asset price dynamics, such as high-frequency responses of clean energy and health care stocks. Taken together, our findings are consistent with markets interpreting changes in the Supreme Court's ideological composition as news about future fiscal expansions or contractions.

Central Bank Economic Transparency and Managerial Learning
Oliver Binz, Elia Ferracuti & Gary Lind
Review of Financial Studies, forthcoming

Abstract:
Central banks increasingly disclose their private information regarding the economy's current and future state (CBET). Consistent with CBET shifting investors' collection and pricing of aggregate-level (where managers do not have an information advantage) toward firm-level (where managers do have an information advantage) information, we find that CBET reduces managers' learning from stock price. The results are (1) pronounced when firms do not provide guidance and when noise trading in firms' stock is low, and (2) robust to using the 2013-2014 amendments to the Bank of England's Inflation Report as an exogenous shock. Additional evidence suggests that CBET lowers investment efficiency.

The Effect of Unrestricted Cash on Lives and Livelihoods: Experimental Evidence from Boston
Ania Jaroszewicz
University of California Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
What is the causal impact of money on well-being? To study this question, we conducted a randomized controlled trial in which we provided monthly unconditional cash transfers -- "no strings attached'' payments -- to a group of low-income Americans. Participants (N=1,486) were randomized to receive either a $360 control payment ($20/month for 18 months) or a non-taxable $9,000 treatment payment ($500/month; 38% increase over total household income). This financial capital treatment was cross-randomized with a social capital treatment that provided participants with tools and encouragement to interact with other participants. Using comprehensive surveys and rich administrative data, we measured outcomes repeatedly over 18 months, focusing on financial effects (spending, savings, debt) and well-being (financial, psychological, health, family well-being). We document a surprising divergence: while cash transfers significantly increased spending and savings, neither the financial nor social capital treatment improved preregistered well-being outcomes. Our estimates rule out even modest positive effects, suggesting that the benefits of cash transfers in high-income countries may be more limited than previously expected. Exploratory, correlational analyses offer three preliminary insights on when money may have comparatively more positive effects on well-being. Cash appears to improve objectively-measured outcomes more than subjectively-measured ones; saving money is more positively correlated with well-being than is spending; and earned income predicts well-being far more strongly than does unearned income. These findings have direct implications for governments, non-profits, and firms supporting financially vulnerable individuals.

Competition and the Cost of U.S. Infrastructure
Lindsey Currier
Harvard Working Paper, September 2026

Abstract:
Can limited competition in procurement auctions explain the high and rising price of road infrastructure in the U.S.? I assemble a new dataset covering the near-universe of state highway auctions between 2002 and 2024. I first document thin competition: one- or two-bidder auctions account for a third of awards, and this share has risen over the past decade. Using spatial variation in inter-state bidder locations, I then estimate the average causal effect of competition on prices; an additional bidder reduces prices by ten percent. To decompose bids into markups and production costs, I develop a structural auction model that incorporates bidders' uncertainty over the number of competitors they face. I show that price increases over the past decade are more attributable to increasing markups than increasing production costs. Limited competition, in turn, is consistent with patterns generated by fixed costs of entering public procurement, but not broad construction-sector fixed costs. Embedding the markup estimates in a structural entry model, I estimate large auction-level -- and even larger market-level -- entry costs, suggesting an important role for procurement bureaucracy and regulatory barriers.

Optimal Taxation of Inflation
Damien Capelle & Yang Liu
American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, October 2026, Pages 64-93

Abstract:
This paper analyzes the effectiveness of a tax on inflation policy (TIP), which would require firms to pay a tax proportional to the increase in their prices or wages, in stabilizing inflation. We show that TIP would effectively correct externalities in firms' pricing decisions, tackle excessive inflation and reduce output volatility. While proposals from the 1970s saw TIP as a substitute for monetary policy (MP), we find that they are complementary, with TIP addressing cost-push shocks, and MP addressing demand shocks. In sharp contrast with price controls, TIP doesn't exacerbate relative price distortions.

Anmol Bhandari & Ellen McGrattan
NBER Working Paper, September 2026

Abstract:
We construct a firm-year panel of income-tax rate reconciliations from annual 10-K filings of public companies to study the effects of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) on U.S. multinational profit shifting. These reconciliations decompose the gap between company-level effective tax rates and the federal statutory corporate tax rate, allowing us to isolate the contribution of foreign tax advantages before and after the reform. We find that TCJA significantly reduced the tax rate gap and increased effective tax rates for companies most exposed to pre-TCJA international tax benefits. This resulted in an onshoring of profits with foreign profit shares falling 1.3 percentage points per percentage point of tax increase. Among more exposed companies, we find no differential change in investment, employment, or the geographic distribution of sales and installed capital. A neoclassical model of a multinational that chooses where to book its income rationalizes this pattern: the reform raised the average tax on income booked abroad relative to income booked at home, which governs where profits are reported, while the marginal tax on capital, which governs investment, changed by an amount common to all firms. Controlling for deferred-tax windfall gains leaves our main results unchanged.

University of Pennsylvania Working Paper, July 2026

Abstract:

We use federal procurement to measure a firm's ideological customer capital attributed to the government and study its asset pricing implications. item.title: Partisan Reality — Polarization and Elections
item.description:
"When they go low, we kick them": The reciprocal nature of citizens' support for democratic transgressions
Lisa Janssen, Hannah Werner & Anna Kern
Journal of Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:

This study examines how citizens respond to democratic transgressions by political opponents and whether they, in turn, support reciprocal transgressions by their own party. Drawing on psychological theories of negative reciprocity, we argue that commitment to democratic principles is relational, shaped by the (un)democratic behavior of other political actors. Through survey experiments in England (N = 4,040) and the United States (N = 4,084), we find that exposure to opponents' transgressions more than doubles citizens' likelihood of endorsing undemocratic actions by their own party. Deductive coding of open-ended responses (N = 907) reveals that many justify reciprocal transgressions as a way to restore fairness and protect democracy from an uneven playing field. Our findings highlight the need for an interactive approach to the study of democratic violations that captures the dynamic and complex nature of citizens' attitudes towards undemocratic behavior.

"Yeah, It's Biased, But ... ": Recognition Versus Moral Condemnation of Bias Across Party Lines
Hannah Waldfogel, Brittany Solomon & Matthew Hall
Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, November 2026, Pages 790-812

Abstract:

Amid rising political polarization, derogatory rhetoric targeting social groups has become common and highly contested across party lines. These partisan divides are often attributed to disagreement about whether bias has occurred, and theories of social norms, harm-based moral judgment, and cognitive consistency suggest that recognizing bias should track moral condemnation. Yet other theories suggest that recognition and condemnation are psychologically distinct. We propose that, even when partisans similarly recognize explicit bias ("yeah, it's biased"), they may diverge in moral response ("but .") -- depending on the target's advantaged or disadvantaged status. Across six prestudies (N = 1,197), eight preregistered experiments (N = 7,145), and 16 supplemental studies, including two preregistered experiments (N = 1,029), we examined this "yeah, but" phenomenon. For speech that partisans equivalently recognized as biased based on race and gender, Democrats condemned bias against disadvantaged targets more than Republicans; Republicans condemned bias against advantaged targets more than Democrats -- patterns that extended to endorsing sanctions (Study 1). Partisans invoked the same justifications -- invulnerability to harm and honesty -- but selectively so, depending on the target (Study 2). These patterns emerged for biases based on socioeconomic status and religion (Studies 3-4), behaviors (Study 5), and partisanship (which lacks a stable status hierarchy; Study 6). However, a status-juxtaposition intervention (judging bias against both advantaged and disadvantaged groups) narrowed Democrats' within-party asymmetry (Studies 7a-b). By disentangling bias recognition from bias condemnation, we show that moral polarization may persist even when Democrats and Republicans both "see" bias and invoke the same moral concerns.

Fit to Print? How Political Bias Affects Media Coverage of Corporate Sociopolitical Activism
Farhan Iqbal, Michael Pfarrer & Abhinav Gupta
Organization Science, forthcoming 

Abstract:

Organizational research has largely treated media coverage of firms as insulated from news outlets' political biases, implicitly assuming that it provides a balanced representation of firm behaviors. However, increasing political polarization and firms' growing involvement in social and political controversies challenge this assumption by creating greater scope for news outlets' political orientations to shape business reporting. We explore this possibility by developing a two-stage framework that discerns news outlets' attention (i.e., what firm behaviors they cover) from their tone (i.e., how they portray those behaviors). We argue that media organizations face two competing pressures: an incentive to cultivate ideological differentiation that appeals to readers and an incentive to maintain credibility that appeals to advertisers. We find that ideological congruence between a news outlet's political orientation and a firm's behavior increases the likelihood that the behavior receives coverage but does not influence the evaluative tone of that coverage -- a pattern we term bias allocation. Supplemental analyses also reveal ideological asymmetries across left- and right-leaning outlets. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for research on the media, organizational political ideology, and strategic management.

Jessica Gottlieb, Damien Kelly & Anne Meng
University of Houston Working Paper, October 2026 

Abstract:

Affective polarization has become a central concern across democracies, raising questions about its consequences for social cohesion and democratic governance. Yet its social consequences may vary across groups. We argue that political exclusion can strengthen group solidarity, reducing the salience of partisan identity, while cross-cutting identities can mitigate the interpersonal consequences of partisan divisions. We test these arguments in the United States using a race-balanced survey and neighbor-choice experiment. We find that Black Americans report less politically induced interpersonal conflict and view polarization as less pressing than White Americans. In our experiment, shared racial identity increases Black respondents' willingness to choose a good outparty neighbor over a bad copartisan neighbor. Exploratory analyses reveal that White Democrats report particularly high levels of interpersonal conflict, concern about polarization, and perceived democratic decline. Alessandro Nai et al.
American Politics Research, forthcoming

Abstract:

Mounting evidence shows the presence of spillover effects of inter-partisan animosity on non-political attitudes, such as social interactions, that are re-interpreted via a partisan lens. Much less clear is whether this spillover effect can also shape cultural preferences or lifestyle choices. In this article we present novel evidence on the relationship between affective polarization and polarized preferences for cats and dogs as pets. That is, we examine the extent in which people showcase a strong preference for their type of pets (e.g., cats) while disliking the other type (e.g., dogs), a phenomenon we term affective PAWlarization. We leverage novel comparative survey evidence gathered from samples of respondents in five countries (The USA, Argentina, Australia, Germany, Italy) in 2022 and 2023, in which we have embedded questions to measure their levels of partisan animosity and a series of innovative measures to tackle polarized pet preferences. Results largely confirm the presence of a positive association between affective polarization and polarized pet preferences, even controlling for several important covariates, albeit not in all countries. Abstract:

We offer a psychological explanation beyond partisan reasoning, positing a systematic tendency among liberals to underestimate the appeal and efficacy of such leaders compared with conservatives. Drawing on moral foundations theory, we propose that liberals' heightened emphasis on harm avoidance and fairness explains their reduced liking for dominance-oriented leaders, and that this reduced likability helps explain why they underestimate these leaders' prospects of success more than conservatives do. We test our predictions across multiple studies, including both political and organizational contexts, demonstrating that political liberals consistently perceive dominance-oriented leaders as less likely to succeed than conservatives do -- even when the leader's political affiliation is irrelevant, unknown, or aligned with their own. We conclude our investigation by suggesting that these diminished expectations from liberals might paradoxically enhance the success trajectories of dominant leaders.

Nicole Huffman, John Kane & David Stack
Research & Politics, October 2026 

Abstract:

With the US Congress increasingly gridlocked, fewer bills are becoming law. Nevertheless, members continue to engage in what we call "symbolic legislating" -- that is, introducing legislation that has effectively no chance of securing enough votes to become law. Despite its prevalence, little is known about the electoral implications of sponsoring symbolic legislation. It is possible that voters reward their legislator's efforts to move the status quo closer to their position even if it has no chance of becoming law. On the other hand, because symbolic legislation is doomed to fail, it may decrease a legislator's perceived effectiveness and, thus, their political support. Alternatively, it is possible that sponsoring symbolic legislation has no impact beyond a cue of the politician's position. In this Research Article, we test these competing hypotheses using a survey experiment. Our experimental results clearly demonstrate that, assuming shared party and issue position, sponsoring symbolic legislation is strongly rewarded. Moreover, the effect is even stronger among voters who are most likely to attend to this information in the real world and operates similarly across parties.

Luca Braghieri, Peter Schwardmann & Egon Tripodi
Carnegie Mellon University Working Paper, October 2026 

Abstract:

We conduct an experiment that engages U.S. Democrats and Republicans in video conversations about policy-relevant facts. Participants prefer co-partisan conversations, believing cross-partisan conversations to be less informative and less pleasant. There is more to learn from counter-partisans, but participants find it harder to extract knowledge from them. Our rich audiovisual data reveal that co- and cross-partisan conversations are strikingly similar in content and tone. Yet, knowledge extraction is impeded by participants' persistent lack of trust in the knowledge of counter-partisans. In contrast, cross-partisan interactions prove more enjoyable than anticipated and significantly reduce affective polarization, an effect that persists in an obfuscated follow-up survey three months later. More emotionally engaged conversations produce larger reductions in affective polarization. Policies encouraging cross-partisan interactions may be more successful at reducing affective polarization than at promoting information aggregation.

Dehua Sun
Social Science Quarterly, September 2026 

Methods: This study examines contact among American undergraduates who naturally interact on campus. By taking advantage of first-year random housing assignments, the analysis compares students with ideological outgroup roommates to those with ideological ingroup roommates. Data come from an original survey at a private university in April 2023.

Results: Students with outgroup roommates report greater favorability toward outgroup students while showing little ideological change, compared to those with ingroup roommates. They also report a higher percentage of ideological outgroup friends and more frequent interactions with them.

Michael Gelman & Anand Goel
University of Delaware Working Paper, September 2026 

Abstract:

The results are consistent with changing perceptions about credit access risk. As the opposing party's candidate won, Democrats became more pessimistic about the future and increasingly concerned about access to credit, leading them to draw on existing credit lines and seek new credit.

item.title: All That Remains — Archaeology and Evidence
item.description:
Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
Rudolf Dellmour et al.
Nature, forthcoming

Abstract:

Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography, particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior. Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained, a pattern not explained by water availability alone. Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement. Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins. Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone. Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.695 to 0.768. Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia. Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.

Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
Rudolf Dellmour et al.
Nature, forthcoming

Abstract:
